newsitem.title: UK: Europe crude outlook - supported by margins, US ar.
newsitem.headline: Europe crude outlook - supported by margins, US ar.

text.p: North Sea crudes will be steady to a bit firmer this week, buoyed by fairly good refinery margins and U.S. demand to replace West African grades snatched up by Asia recently, traders said.

They said Brent was likely to keep gains it posted most of last week when it gained 10 cents a barrel between Monday and Wednesday before softening slightly on Thursday. Other grades should maintain current levels also.
"There is good demand for physical barrels...so I will go for a balanced market for Europe and prices moving sideways to slightly higher," one trader said.
A refiner said he saw the Brent market remaining "fairly steady", backed by good refining margins and a good Brent-WTI spread, currently at about $1.60.
The traders said they saw no reason why the differentials on the other North Sea grades would go up.
Forties and Ekofisk gained three cents on Thursday to trade Dated Brent +23 cents and +16 cents respectively, while Statfjord last fetched Dated +18/+20 on April 25.
"I see the current figures as tops on the differentials, I cannot see them getting much stronger," the refiner said.
"But the margins are looking good, gas oil is looking good and cracks are looking good," he said.

However, one grade, Norwegian sweet Oseberg, will most likely continue to be pressured, suffering from excess unsold avails. It was talked some four cents weaker at about Dated Brent +10 cents, traders said.
"Yes, there's quite a few (Oseberg cargoes) on offer...It looks like there should be more than 15 (cargoes) on offer," one European crude buyer said.
A European buyer, seconding the view most North Sea grades would remain steady for the May 5-9 week, said: "The supply/demand picture is in balance at the moment".
He said the European market could be propped up by possible increased U.S. demand, to fill the gap left by West African crudes picked up by Asian buyers recently.
"They (United States) need to buy 8.5 million barrels a day, so there's usually good demand from the United States" the refiner said.

"But what happened on the May programme was that the Far East took a lot of West African (crude), so some of the traditional West African grades that used to go to the United States will now be substituted I guess with North Sea barrels mainly," he added.

Mediterranean and West African crude markets are expected to remain fairly quiet this week but traders see some split in sentiment with deteriorating refining margins keeping Mediterranean buyers quiet while good Asian and transatlantic demand continued to support West African crude.
"The deteriorating margins will dampen Mediterranean refiner buying, but avails are not too lengthy so sellers can stay relaxed for a while," one trade said.
Traders expect lighter West African grades to stay supported by ongoing demand from Far East refiners topping up after a recent lengthy spell of maintenance and transatlantic buying.
But prices for distillate rich Forcados could slip a little if supportive demand from Mediterranean refiners starts to subside.
Buying for June FOB barrels will become the focus of interest with May cargoes mostly tied up.
"The market should stay pretty firm in the near term but we May see the usual price volatility when NNPC starts pricing for June," one trader said.
At the end of last week Forcados was valued steady around dated Brent +10 cents a barrel while Bonny Light was valued around dated Brent +47 cents a barrel.
The narrower refining margins pegged Russian Urals crude slightly softer at the end of last week. Prompt barrels valued around dated Brent -$1.
-- H. Haddadin, London newsroom +44 171 542 8145
